newsitem.title: USA: Jurors say they can judge U.S. bomb suspect fairly.
newsitem.headline: Jurors say they can judge U.S. bomb suspect fairly.

text.p: Most potential jurors quizzed so far in the trial of accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh say they can do what the defence calls impossible -- judge him fairly despite a torrent of pre-trial publicity.

Nearly all of the 13 people questioned during the first two days of jury selection have said they were deeply shocked by the April 19, 1995, blast that destroyed the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, killing 168 people and injuring hundreds.
And most say they could not avoid the intense media coverage of the arrest of McVeigh, a 28-year-old Gulf War veteran, and the investigation of the worst bombing attack on civilians in U.S. history.
With a few exceptions, however, most potential jurors questioned so far say they could set aside the reports and judge McVeigh fairly on the evidence put before them at trial.
McVeigh could face the death penalty if convicted in the trial being held in a tightly guarded federal court in Denver.

He and former army buddy Terry Nichols, who will be tried separately later, have pleaded not guilty to the attack, which prosecutors say was in revenge for the deaths of at least 80 people in a federal raid on the Branch Davidian sect compound in Waco, Texas, exactly two years earlier.

Most potential jurors who knew about recent news reports alleging that McVeigh had confessed his guilt to his attorneys said they would not be swayed by them. Several voiced scepticism about media reports on Tuesday.

"Anybody can create a document and say there's a confession," one potential juror said when asked about highly publicised reports of McVeigh's alleged confession in the Dallas Morning News and Playboy magazine -- reports that have been adamantly denied by his attorneys.

Asked if he could put the stories and other media coverage out of his mind if called upon to sit in judgment of McVeigh, the young man, who worked in the environmental field, said: "I don't think that would be a problem at all."

A philosophy teacher who amused the audience by criticising the phrasing of juror survey questions said he did not believe that a news report of the alleged confession had affected his ability to judge McVeigh.
But a commercial artist said she could not put the images of the 19 children killed in the blast out of her mind. She also said she believed McVeigh was guilty based on the news reports she had read.
McVeigh's attorneys tried last week to have the trial delayed, saying its outcome had been "preordained" because of the media reports about McVeigh.

They said in a court filing that McVeigh would be convicted and sentenced to death because "the minds of prospective jurors have been irreversibly poisoned." A federal appeals court last week turned down the request for a delay.

U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch, prosecutors and defence attorneys have closely questioned potential jurors, dissecting their opinions on the bombing, the federal government and their attitude toward the death penalty.

A testy Matsch snapped at lawyers several times on Tuesday as he tried to hurry along the proceedings, but legal experts say it could still take weeks to seat a jury of 12 people and six alternates from a pool that now numbers around 350.
On Tuesday, Matsch dismissed a prospective juror who feared she would break down under the stress of a long trial.

The defence will likely seek to disqualify potential jurors they think are prejudiced against McVeigh, while prosecutors are expected to be wary of jurors with a grievance against the government. Potential jurors with serious health problems or who would suffer severe economic hardship if they served throughout a long trial will also be excused.
McVeigh, looking like a college student in a button-down blue shirt and pressed khaki pants, has followed proceedings closely, laughing loudly when jokes are made.
